Visualizing the unseen (until I get hired): a model that was never told about environmental justice found an environmental-justice pattern anyway.

Merascope ranks every US ZIP code into 10 tiers by how closely it resembles a place that already hosts a data center. The model behind that ranking sees only real infrastructure and geography -- grid proximity, terrain, contamination sites, community demographics, population density -- and one boolean label: does this ZIP already host a facility. It's never told what "environmental justice" is, never given a fairness objective, never scored on anything but pattern-matching to existing hosts. So I asked what tier 10 -- the ZIPs the model thinks look most like data-center country -- actually looks like on the ground, next to tier 1.

The grid-access story is exactly what you'd expect: tier 10 ZIPs sit far closer to transmission lines (proximity score 0.60 -> 0.97 from tier 1 to tier 10) and substations (0.36 -> 0.86). But riding along with that, unasked: tier 10 ZIPs also sit far closer to Superfund and RCRA hazardous-waste sites (the "far from contamination" score falls from 0.39 to 0.04, "far from RCRA site" from 0.59 to 0.04) and carry a much heavier environmental-justice burden (0.90 -> 0.49). Checked for breadth, not just a couple of dense clusters skewing the national average: 48 of 48 states individually show the same tier-1-to-tier-10 gap on contamination proximity.

One honest caveat, because it matters for how to read this: the EJ line isn't a fully independent third proof next to the RCRA and contamination lines it's plotted with -- Merascope's real EJ formula is demographic burden (poverty + minority rate) multiplied by the mean of those same hazard scores, so it shares real math with two of the other lines by construction. What is genuinely independent is population density, and it moves the same direction anyway (0.965 -> 0.44) -- so the pattern isn't just one indicator counted three times, it's grid access trading against both hazard proximity and density along the same axis.

The model was never asked to find any of this. It was asked one question -- "does this ZIP look like a place that already has a data center" -- using features that don't include EJ score, contamination score, or population at all in its training target. That the answer it reconstructs, purely from grid and terrain similarity, lines up this cleanly with community burden isn't the model's bias. It's the landscape's: in the real, already-built geography of American power infrastructure, proximity to the grid and proximity to burden are the same place.

NOTES
%%%%%

Data: Merascope's own public risk model and 22-indicator siting pipeline (merascope.com/#/risk), 33,252 US ZCTAs. Tiers are out-of-fold predicted probabilities from a `has_dc` classifier (spatially-blocked cross-validation, prediction discarded, only the probability kept), rank-cut into 10 equal-count bins -- the same method the live product uses. Tier-by-tier means are the full national average at each tier, not a subsample. State-breadth check (48/48 states) uses the same contamination_score_nat column, median gap 0.38.

Images: dc_tier_composition_profile.png (national mean of each indicator by tier, two panels -- hazard/EJ/density falling, grid access rising) + dc_tier_composition_corr.png (all indicators ranked by Spearman correlation with tier, for anyone who wants the full list past the six charted).

### AI usage:
Built with Claude Code, Simon-Hans Edasi directing. Simon walked through the model mechanics himself -- boolean target, probability kept not the prediction, rank-cut into tiers -- and asked directly whether the EJ line in the chart was really an independent signal or partly just measuring population density. Neither guess was quite right: Claude checked the actual pipeline source (`scripts/zcta/rescore_ej.py`) instead of assuming, and found ej_score is a composite of demographic burden times mean hazard-proximity score, with no population-density term in it at all -- density is a fully separate indicator that happens to move the same direction. That correction is folded into the caveat paragraph above rather than left out. Earlier in the same build, the profile chart itself went through two real revisions on Simon's direction: first dropping star/diamond rural/urban markers that were cluttering a chart meant to be about tiers, not the rural/urban split (a separate finding, covered in earlier posts in this series); then moving both panels' legends below the plot after the first version's legend sat directly on top of the lines it was labeling.
